answer.summary: Atawodi recommends grounding teams in customer problems through direct product use and a shared, regularly updated problem list. Bring stakeholder perspectives into strategy, then synthesize and prioritize the problems so the team has clarity about what it is solving.

sections.heading: Build a shared view of the problems
sections.content: Start by empathizing with customers and the problem: put yourself in users’ shoes, develop a visual understanding of their difficulties, and actually use the product. Atawodi also recommends paying attention to products you value and articulating what works; exposure and curiosity help refine product sense. She describes a living “top 10 things you should know” document for each PM, listing known product problems. Problems can be qualitative, quantitative, and include tech debt; revise the document every quarter.

sections.heading: Include stakeholders, then curate
sections.content: For strategy sessions, Atawodi sometimes asks stakeholders—such as marketing or operations—to submit and stack-rank their own 10 problems using the same template. She also gathers perspectives from communications, support, research, and content strategy. Then the PM’s work is to synthesize those different views (“sandpapering down” to the core) and curate the problems together, providing clarity and context about what is being solved. One example insight was that the average reading age of an American is 11, prompting consideration of images or video instead of text.

sections.heading: Keep the shared understanding focused
sections.content: Although the working document can contain 10 problems, Atawodi says she starts with 10 and often ends up with three; in presentations she may distill the key takeaways into a few numbers or insights. This is a way to make the most important problems memorable, not a claim that every team must use exactly three.

judgment.explanation: The answer accurately describes the living, regularly revised list of product problems and gathering stakeholder input to synthesize and prioritize problems. However, it omits the reference’s specific practice of bringing product, design/UX, data, and engineering partners together to review, discuss, and vote on the problems, so it does not cover all expected points.

It usefully addresses how to build a shared understanding, but it does not cover the expected detail of bringing product, design, data, and engineering partners together to review, discuss, and prioritize the problems. The cited context supports collaborative input and curation, but not that specific cross-functional review process.
